title: Flaviviruses (Dengue, Yellow Fever, Japanese Encephalitis, West Nile, Zika)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of severe headache and a 1-day history of neck and shoulder pain, light and sound sensitivity, slight nausea, lower back pain, and a headache “all over.” He denied any recent travel, tick bites, rashes, chest pain, or shortness of breath. On examination, a faint erythematous rash was noted over his chest, he had a fever (38°C), and neck stiffness. A lumbar puncture was performed and the following results were reported: Total protein, CSF 53 (15–45 mg/dL) Glucose, CSF 56 (40–70 mg/dL) Xanthochromia Absent RBC, CSF 37/μ L Nucleated Cells, CSF 50 (0–5/μ L) PMN 14% Lymphocytes 51% Monocyte/ Macrophage 34% Plasma cell 1% Gram stain PMNs seen, no organisms seen
questions.lead_in: What test is most likely to be diagnostic?

options.text: Bacterial culture of the CSF for Neisseria meningitidis
NAAT testing for West Nile virus infection from the blood
NAAT testing of the CSF for enterovirus
Streptococcus pneumoniae antigen test of the CSF

questions.explanation: NAAT testing of the CSF for enterovirus This patient was diagnosed with enterovirus disease. Though it is possible to culture enterovirus from the CSF , the rapid turnaround time and exquisite sensitivity and specificity of NAAT testing make it the test of choice. The CSF profile doesn’t fit the typical profile for bacterial meningitis as the protein and glucose were both normal (you typically expect decreased glucose and increased protein in bacterial meningitis). NAAT testing for viruses is the appropriate method to use in most cases. One of the exceptions is West Nile virus because the level of viremia usually drops to very low, if not undetectable, levels by the time of symptom onset. Ebola virus is not realistic in this case as the patient has had no travel history.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q3

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of sore throat, fever, headache, and myalgia. He had returned from a week-long trip to the Caribbean 6 days earlier. He was normally well and did not take any regular medications. On physical examination, his temperature was 38°C (100.9°F), blood pressure 102/70 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/minute, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. His pharynx was injected, but no exudate was seen. He had a maculopapular rash on his chest, back, and extremities, sparing the palms and soles. Investigations: Total white cell count 3.1 ×109/L Platelet count 81 ×109/L Hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL Total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL (22 μmol/L) ALT 121 U/L AST 163 U/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dengue The patient has signs and symptoms of dengue fever and recently traveled to a highly endemic area. Think of dengue in any febrile traveler returning from endemic regions. For your boards, remember key differences between yellow fever (more transaminitis and jaundice, lack of immunization prior to travel), chikungunya (more joint disease, less plasma leakage), and leptospirosis (water exposure, conjunctival suffusion). Disease Dengue Chikungunya Yellow Fever Leptospirosis What to look for: Febrile illness, mosquito exposure Thrombocytopenia Shock Febrile illness, mosquito exposure Joint pains Milder disease than dengue Febrile illness, mosquito exposure Transaminitis, jaundice, no vaccine prior to travel Febrile illness, water exposure Hyperbilirubinemia out of proportion to transaminitis Conjunctival suffusion
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q27

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of low grade fever, malaise, itchy eyes, and a widespread itchy, maculopapular rash. She had returned from a 4-week holiday in the Caribbean 2 days before her symptoms began.
questions.lead_in: What vector is most likely to be responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Aedes mosquito This is most likely to be Zika infection, but could easily be dengue or chikungunya. Aedes aegypti is the main vector in transmission of all three viruses, but Aedes albopictus is also responsible for spreading disease. The mosquito feeds largely during the day but may still bite at night. The principal method of protection is bite avoidance with the use of personal protective measures, such as insect repellents and attempts to remove potential breeding sites for mosquitos in urban areas.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q26

questions.stem: During an outbreak of West Nile virus (WNV) in late summer in northern Texas, a 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, headache, abdominal pain, myalgias, and anorexia. She had attended the emergency department as she had noticed difficulty in walking and twitching of her thigh muscles in the preceding 24 hours. On examination she had reduced power grade 3/5 in left hip flexion and knee extension, absent deep tendon reflexes in both lower limbs, and widespread generalized fasciculations. Sensory examination was normal. CSF microscopy: Total protein 0.55 g/L (0.15–0.45) Glucose 4.1 mmol/L (3.3–4.4) White cell count 0.34 ×109/L (≤5), 70% polymorphs CSF PCR panel HSV-1+2/VZV/enterovirus/echovirus/WNV negative Acute serum: WNV IgM antibody positive Convalescent serum: significantly high titer of neutralizing antibodies to WNV (1: 320) MRI: spine ill-defined nonenhancing hyperintensity in the cervicothoracic cord
questions.lead_in: What is the likelihood that she will recover strength to near baseline?
questions.explanation: 35% Among patients with acute flaccid paralysis, about one-third recover strength to near baseline, one-third have some improvement, and one-third have little or no improvement. Treatment of WNV infection is supportive. Several investigated therapeutic approaches, including ribavirin, steroids, IVIG, and monoclonal antibodies, have failed to demonstrate efficacy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q47

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted in the late summer with several days of fever and headache, followed by altered mental status and progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness. On exam, he had flaccid paralysis of both legs, with some muscle fasciculations. CSF analysis showed 450 nucleated cells with 75% lymphocytes, normal glucose, and protein of 80. Brain MRI showed some T2-weighted abnormalities in his basal ganglia.
questions.lead_in: What type of virus is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Flavivirus This patient most likely has infection with West Nile virus. He is presenting with meningoencephalitis with prominent peripheral neurologic sequelae. Other Flaviviridae-associated diseases include St. Louis encephalitis virus, dengue, Japanese encephalitis virus, and yellow fever virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q32

questions.question: A GP has a patient who presents with fever, fatigue and macular rash. It is autumn. He sends for West Nile serology. Recent testing: WNV IgM positive, WNV IgG positive, WNV IgG avidity high. One year ago: WNV IgM positive, WNV IgG positive, WNV IgG avidity low.
questions.question_raw: A GP has a patient who presents with fever, fatigue and macular rash. It is Autumn. He sends for West Nile Serology. Recent testing: WNV IgM: +, WNV IgG: +, WNV IgG avidity: high. 1 year ago: WNV IgM: +, WNV IgG: +, WNV IgG avidity: low.

parts.text: Interpret and provide two reasons why it is unlikely to be acute WNV. Does he have WNV?

parts_raw.text: Interpret and provide 2 reasons why it's unlikely to be acute WNV. Does he have WNV?

questions.model_answer: Interpretation: serologic evidence of past West Nile virus infection acquired approximately one year ago (when IgG avidity was low, i.e. recently matured), not an acute infection now. Yes, he has been infected with WNV, but the current febrile/rash illness is unlikely to be caused by acute WNV. Two reasons it is unlikely to be acute: (1) High IgG avidity indicates a matured antibody response from remote infection, whereas acute infection produces low-avidity IgG (as seen one year ago). (2) WNV IgM persists long after infection—for longer than 16 months in some West Nile encephalitis patients—so a positive IgM alone is only presumptive and does not indicate acute infection, especially where asymptomatic infection is common.
questions.beyond_mandell: IgG avidity maturation (low = recent, high = remote) is general serologic immunology; not detailed in this chapter.

questions.question: Give two measures to prevent transmission of locally acquired Zika virus.

parts.text: Give two measures to prevent transmission of locally acquired Zika.

parts_raw.text: Give two measures to prevent transmission of locally acquired Zika.

questions.model_answer: (1) Personal mosquito-bite avoidance: wear long sleeves and pants, apply insect repellent, and stay indoors in areas protected by window screens and mosquito nets. (2) Environmental vector control to eliminate Aedes breeding sites, particularly reduction/covering of standing-water containers and tanks.

cohort_answer.text: Condom use; DEET or other prevention of mosquito bites; Mosquito control

questions.model_answer: a) The wait is governed by the male partner: 3 months after return (the female partner alone would wait 2 months), so a couple waits 3 months. b) 21 days after return before donating blood. c) A woman with confirmed/symptomatic Zika should wait 2 months after symptom onset before attempting to conceive. d) Barrier precautions (condoms) or abstinence for the entire duration of the pregnancy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Waiting periods and blood-donation deferral are from PHAC/CDC preconception guidance and Canadian Blood Services, not from this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: Zika virus.

parts.text: What percentage of patients are symptomatic?
List four ways it is transmitted.
List three neurologic complications in adults.

parts_raw.text: a) what % of patients are symptomatic?
list 4 ways to transmit

questions.model_answer: a) Approximately 20% are symptomatic (about 80% of infections are asymptomatic). b) Four routes of transmission: (1) mosquito bite (Aedes aegypti/albopictus) (2) sexual transmission (virus concentrated in semen, detectable up to ~62 days) (3) vertical/perinatal (maternal-fetal, placental) (4) blood transfusion. c) Three adult neurologic complications: (1) Guillain-Barré syndrome (2) meningoencephalitis/encephalitis (3) myelitis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only GBS is emphasized in the chapter; meningoencephalitis and myelitis as adult neurologic complications are supported by broader IDSA/CDC descriptions.
questions.cohort_conflict: Text gives ~20% symptomatic (80% asymptomatic); cohort's 25% differs slightly from the chapter figure.

cohort_answer.text: 25% symptomatic. Transmission: Mosquitoes, Sexual, Vertical, Blood transfusion (no documented breastmilk transmission but theoretical risk). Neurologic complications: Encephalitis, Uveitis, Guillain Barre (also CIDP, ADEM, myelitis)

questions.question: Yellow fever vaccine.

parts.text: What 2 adverse events are associated with this vaccine and which age groups are most high risk?
Who should get a booster dose? Name 3

parts_raw.text: What 2 adverse events are associated with this vaccine and which age groups are most high risk?
Who should get a booster dose? Name 3

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Yellow fever vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND: meningoencephalitis, ADEM, Guillain-Barre) - highest risk at the extremes of age, infants <9 months and adults >=60 years, particularly on first dose. (2) Yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease (YEL-AVD: multiorgan failure resembling wild-type yellow fever) - highest risk in adults >=60 years (rising further >70), and in those with thymus disease/thymectomy.
b) A single dose is considered protective for life for most travellers; a booster is indicated in: (1) women vaccinated while pregnant; (2) persons vaccinated while HIV-infected/immunosuppressed, and recipients of HSCT after vaccination; (3) those first vaccinated as infants/children <2 years of age; also laboratory workers with ongoing exposure and travellers with ongoing high-risk exposure whose last dose was >10 years ago.
questions.beyond_mandell: WHO/IHR 2016 and CDC Yellow Book: single dose confers lifelong validity, with the listed groups as booster exceptions.

What are two contraindications?
What do you tell someone going to an endemic area who is not allowed to have vaccine (2) – (2011)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Africa (sub-Saharan, tropical belt); (2) South America (tropical regions - Amazon basin of Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia).
b) (1) YEL-AND (neurotropic disease: meningoencephalitis, ADEM, GBS) - highest risk in infants <9 months and in adults >=60 years, first dose. (2) YEL-AVD (viscerotropic disease with multiorgan failure) - highest risk in adults >=60 years and those with thymus disorders/prior thymectomy.
c) (1) Vaccinated during pregnancy; (2) vaccinated while HIV-infected/immunosuppressed, or HSCT after prior vaccination; (3) first dose given at <2 years of age; also laboratory workers with continued exposure, and travellers whose last dose was >10 years ago heading to prolonged high-risk exposure.
d) (1) Age <6 months (relative <9 months) - risk of YEL-AND; (2) immunocompromise: symptomatic HIV/CD4 <200, thymus disorder or thymectomy, haematologic malignancy, transplant, high-dose steroids or biologics. Anaphylaxis to eggs/gelatin/vaccine components is also a contraindication.
e) (1) Provide a medical waiver letter for the International Certificate, and advise deferring or avoiding travel to endemic rural areas, especially in peak transmission season. (2) Rigorous mosquito bite avoidance against day-biting Aedes: DEET or icaridin repellent, permethrin-treated long sleeves and trousers, screened/air-conditioned accommodation and bed nets; note entry may be refused at some borders.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Yellow Book/WHO IHR yellow fever vaccination recommendations.

cohort_answer.text: Continents: South America (tropical regions); Sub-Saharan Africa. Side effects: Yellow fever vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND); Yellow fever vaccine associated viscerotropic disease (YEL-AVD). Booster indicated: First dose <2y; Risk laboratory personnel; Post HSCT; Vaccine >10 years ago and plan to spend prolonged period in endemic areas during peak transmission season. Contraindications: Immunocompromised host; Known egg allergy. Advice if not vaccinated: Avoid travel if possible or rural endemic areas; Mosquito repellent, long sleeves, bed net

questions.question: A patient with dengue.

parts.text: Explain the pathophysiology of the hemorrhagic fever.
What is associated with more severe disease?
What are two WHO findings in dengue with warning signs that require close monitoring?

parts_raw.text: Explain the pathophysiology of the hemorrhagic fever?
What is associated with more severe disease?
What are 2 WHO findings in Dengue with warning signs that require close monitoring

questions.model_answer: a) Dengue hemorrhagic fever is immune-mediated: a secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype leads to antibody-dependent enhancement and a cytokine response that produces increased vascular (capillary) permeability with plasma leakage and abnormal hemostasis/bleeding—the two defining mechanisms—manifesting as hemoconcentration (rising hematocrit), effusions, hypotension and hemorrhage. b) More severe disease is associated with secondary heterologous DENV infection (prior exposure to a different serotype), certain serotypes, extremes of age (infants and the elderly), and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, and pulmonary or cardiac disease. c) Two WHO warning signs mandating close monitoring: (1) abdominal pain/tenderness (2) persistent vomiting (others: mucosal bleeding, lethargy/mental-status change, decreased urine output, narrowing pulse pressure, rising hematocrit).

questions.question: Dengue hemorrhagic fever: pathophysiology, risk factors, and sentinel signs of deterioration.
questions.question_raw: 10) Dengue hemorrhagic fever: pathophys, risk factors, sentinel signs of deterioration

parts.text: Dengue hemorrhagic fever: pathophysiology, risk factors, sentinel signs of deterioration.

parts_raw.text: Dengue hemorrhagic fever: pathophys, risk factors, sentinel signs of deterioration

questions.model_answer: Pathophysiology: immune-mediated. Secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype drives antibody-dependent enhancement and a cytokine response causing increased capillary permeability with plasma leakage and hemorrhage (rising hematocrit, effusions, hypotension). Risk factors for severe disease: secondary heterologous DENV infection, DENV serotype, infants and elderly, and comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, pulmonary/cardiac disease). Sentinel signs of deterioration (WHO warning signs): abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy or mental-status change, decreased urine output, tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, mucosal bleeding, and an increase in hematocrit of >20% (indicating significant plasma leakage).

questions.question: Japanese encephalitis.

parts.text: What are three things to ask prior to travel for vaccination?
How long does it take to produce an immune response?

parts_raw.text: What are 3 things to ask prior to travel for vaccination?
How long does it take to produce an immune response?

questions.model_answer: a) Three things to ask (ACIP risk assessment): (1) Duration of travel—is the trip ≥1 month, or shorter but during the transmission season, to a JE-endemic area? (2) Destination—rural/agricultural areas, known outbreak areas, or open-ended itinerary versus urban-only travel? (3) Planned activities and accommodation—outdoor or evening exposure and lodging without bed nets (higher risk). b) The two-dose primary series (IXIARO, days 0 and 28) should be completed at least one week before travel or potential exposure to ensure a protective immune response.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort states an immune response 'within 60 days'; the chapter's licensed inactivated vaccine (IXIARO) requires the series completed ≥1 week before exposure, so the answer is grounded in that.

cohort_answer.text: Things to ask: Travel to endemic country >1 month or frequent travellers; <1 month but during summer/fall, also based on location/activities/accommodations; indicated for recurrent travel (>1mo) to endemic areas (Far East/SE Asia rice growing regions), known JE outbreak region, laboratory worker at risk, or <1mo stay with extensive outdoor activities. CI in hypersensitivity to protamine sulfate, history of urticaria, or <2mo of age. Immune response time: within 60 days of immunization.

questions.model_answer: a) Genus Flavivirus (family Flaviviridae). b) Four other flaviviruses: (1) Dengue virus (2) Yellow fever virus (3) Japanese encephalitis virus (4) West Nile virus. c) Vector: Aedes mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus; originally isolated from Aedes africanus). d) Four classic symptoms: (1) rash (2) fever (3) arthralgia (4) non-purulent conjunctivitis. e) Approximately 20% of infected patients develop symptoms (about 80% asymptomatic).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort lists hepatitis C virus in this genus; HCV is genus Hepacivirus, not the mosquito-borne genus Flavivirus, and the chapter gives ~20% symptomatic rather than the cohort's 25%.

cohort_answer.text: Genus: Flavivirus (single strand RNA). Other viruses: Hepatitis C, Dengue, Yellow Fever, Japanese Encephalitis (also West Nile, St. Louis). Vector: Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus (daytime biters). Classic symptoms: Fever (65%), Pruritic Macular Rash (90%), Headache (45%), Arthralgia (65%), Myalgia (48%). Symptomatic percentage: 25%

questions.question: Yellow fever.

parts.text: What are two continents where travel-related vaccination against yellow fever should be considered?
What are two adverse effects of the vaccine and the age groups at highest risk for each?
What are three indications for a booster dose of yellow fever vaccine?

parts_raw.text: What are two continents where travel related vaccination against Yellow Fever should be considered?
What are two adverse effects of the vaccine and the age groups at highest risk for each?
What are three indications for a booster dose of YFV?

questions.model_answer: a) Two continents: Africa and South America (at-risk endemic countries). b) Two serious adverse effects: (1) Yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease (YEL-AVD)—highest risk in older adults (≥60 years) and those with thymus disorders. (2) Yellow fever vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND)—highest risk at the extremes of age: infants (vaccine contraindicated <4 months, cautioned 4-9 months) and older adults. c) Three booster indications: (1) travelers who received their dose >10 years ago and will have prolonged exposure in an endemic area or travel to an ongoing outbreak; (2) at-risk laboratory workers handling yellow fever virus; (3) immunocompromised persons, including HIV-infected individuals (with uncontrolled HIV replication needing earlier boosting) and women who were pregnant when they received their first dose.

cohort_answer.text: Continents: South America, Africa. Adverse effects: YEL-AND (yellow fever vaccine-associated neurotropic disease) - highest risk in infants <6 months and >70 years old; YEL-AVD (viscerotropic disease) - up to 6x higher risk in those ≥60 years old, also individuals with thymus disorders (thymoma, MG, thymectomy), HIV/AIDS (CD4<200), on immunosuppressive therapies. Booster indications: at-risk lab personnel handling YF (10-year booster), travelers (consider one-time booster per CATMAT 2018), pregnant women at time of vaccination, HSCT recipients since vaccination, HIV-infected persons (q10 years), those whose last dose was ≥10 years ago and at high risk (prolonged endemic region stay, travel to highly endemic area like West Africa).

questions.question: Name two ways to limit autochthonous (locally acquired) spread of Zika virus in Canada.

parts.text: Name two ways to limit autochthonous spread of Zika virus in Canada

parts_raw.text: Name two ways to limit autochthonous spread of Zika virus in Canada

questions.model_answer: (1) Vector control: surveillance for and suppression of competent Aedes mosquitoes (source reduction of standing-water breeding sites, larviciding/adulticiding) so an introduced viremic traveller cannot seed local mosquito transmission. (2) Interrupt non-vector transmission: defer blood/tissue donation from returning travellers and screen the blood supply, and advise condom use/abstinence after travel to prevent sexual transmission (protecting pregnant partners in particular).
questions.beyond_mandell: Control measures rest on PHAC/CATMAT and Canadian Blood Services guidance, not the Mandell chapter.

How long should you wait before donating blood?

questions.model_answer: a) Females: wait at least 2 months after return/last possible exposure (or symptom onset) before trying to conceive. b) Males: wait at least 3 months after return/last exposure (or symptom onset). c) Blood donation: defer, typically ~21 days after leaving the risk area (per Canadian Blood Services). d) Use condoms (or abstain) for the entire remaining duration of the pregnancy. e) An infected woman should wait at least 2 months from symptom onset before conceiving.
questions.beyond_mandell: Waiting intervals and donation deferral are CDC/CATMAT/Canadian Blood Services recommendations; the chapter states only that men with a pregnant partner should abstain or use condoms (p. 2024) without giving the specific intervals.

cohort_answer.text: A) CATMAT no longer routinely recommends avoiding travel; if Zika confirmed, women wait at least 2 months, male partners at least 3 months after return/symptom onset before trying to conceive/unprotected sex; if positive male, avoid sex for remainder of pregnancy. B) 21 day waiting period after travel generally; 14 days if from Europe/US/Antarctica; if travel to malaria endemic area 3 months if there 1 day-6 months, 3 years if there >6 months; UK 1980-1996 cumulative 3+ months excluded for vCJD. C) Risk considered low; CATMAT no longer recommends routine measures for asymptomatic travellers; if confirmed/symptomatic male partner, recommend abstain from unprotected sex for duration of pregnancy; otherwise no condoms recommended. D) 2 months from start of symptoms OR 2 months since returning from travel, whichever is later.

parts_raw.text: Describe the single main pathophysiology process for severe dengue
Describe circumstance that predispose an individual to severe dengue
List 2 warning signs as per WHO criteria that increase progression to severe Dengue

questions.model_answer: a) Antibody-dependent enhancement: non-neutralizing heterologous antibody from a prior infection with a different DENV serotype binds virus and enhances its uptake/replication in Fc-receptor-bearing monocytes, driving a robust memory T-cell and cytokine response (TNF-alpha, IL-2, IFN-gamma) plus complement activation that produces transient vascular endothelial dysfunction and plasma leakage. b) A secondary (sequential) infection with a heterologous DENV serotype (relative risk for DHF/shock up to ~100 vs primary infection); also infants who passively acquire maternal DENV antibody. c) Any two of: (1) severe abdominal pain, (2) persistent vomiting, (3) mucosal bleeding, (4) clinical fluid accumulation/plasma leakage, (5) lethargy.

cohort_answer.text: Pathophysiology: Antibody dependent enhancement from previous exposure where heterophilic antibodies from another serotype of dengue recognize and bind to new dengue virus, causing massive cytokine response without neutralizing infection, causing increased vascular permeability and plasma leakage causing shock in severe cases. Predisposing circumstance: Prior infection with dengue, age <5. Warning signs: Severe abdominal pain; Persistent vomiting; Clinical fluid accumulation; Mucosal bleeding; Lethargy/aLOC; Hepatomegaly >2cm; Increased hematocrit, decreasing platelet count

questions.question: Japanese encephalitis.

parts.text: Three things to ask about the travel history.
How long to produce an immune response (vaccine).

parts_raw.text: A. 3 things to ask about travel
B. How long to produce an immune response

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Destination and setting: which country/region in endemic Asia and whether rural/agricultural (rice-paddy and pig-farming areas, where Culex vectors and amplifying pigs/birds concentrate risk) versus urban. (2) Timing/season of travel (temperate areas transmit chiefly July-September; subtropical/tropical areas year-round). (3) Duration of stay and outdoor/evening activities (vectors feed outdoors in the evening; longer rural stays raise the otherwise low traveller risk). b) The inactivated JE vaccine (IXIARO) is a 2-dose IM series on days 0 and 28; the series should be completed at least ~1 week (10 days) before exposure, with protective antibody in ~95% about a week after the second dose.
questions.beyond_mandell: The vaccine schedule and time-to-protection (part b) are from the product monograph/CATMAT-ACIP guidance, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Location: Country (SE Asia, China, India, Nepal, northern tip of Australia), rural agricultural areas with flooding irrigation (Culex mosquito larvae develop in standing water such as rice fields, virus transmitted from infected hosts i.e. pigs and wild birds, not humans). Duration of exposure: incubation 5-15 days. Season: peaks in summer/fall in temperate areas, sporadic or year-round in tropics. Activities: outdoor (camping/hiking/cycling/fieldwork) esp evening/night when mosquitoes active. Also: immunization status, protection against mosquitoes.

B) In Canada, IXIARO (inactivated JE vaccine), approved for 2 months and above. A series of two doses (IM) given on days 0 and 28; series should be completed 10-14 days before potential exposure to develop adequate antibody response. Booster dose after 12 months for those at risk. A single dose induces protective antibodies in 30% of vaccinees at 10 days and 40% at 28 days; a second dose at 28 days induces antibodies in ~95% of vaccinees at 28 days after the second dose. Protective antibody concentration declines over time, with 60-80% of fully immunized vaccinees maintaining adequate antibodies at 12 months.

questions.question: Yellow fever vaccine.

parts.text: Side effects of yellow fever vaccine, including the worst one.
What are two contraindications to the yellow fever vaccine?
What do you tell someone going to an endemic area who is not allowed to have the vaccine?

parts_raw.text: A) Side effects of Yellow Fever vaccine (worst one?)
B) What are 2 contraindications to the yellow fever vaccine?
C) What do you tell someone going to an endemic area who is not allowed to have the vaccine?

questions.model_answer:
a) Common/mild: injection site soreness, low-grade fever, headache and myalgia in 10–30%, 5–10 days post-vaccination. Serious: immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (egg or gelatin, ~1.3/100,000). The two severe syndromes are YEL-AND (vaccine-associated neurotropic disease — meningoencephalitis, ADEM, Guillain-Barré syndrome, bulbar palsy; onset 3–28 days; ~0.8/100,000, higher at the extremes of age; usually recovers) and, the worst, YEL-AVD (vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease — a yellow-fever-like multi-organ failure syndrome with hepatitis, renal failure, coagulopathy and shock, onset 2–5 days after a first dose, ~0.3–0.4/100,000 but higher over age 60, case fatality about 50–65%; associated with thymic disease).

b) (1) Infants under 6 months of age (risk of vaccine-associated encephalitis). (2) Immunosuppression — symptomatic HIV or CD4 <200, hematologic or generalized malignancy, transplant recipients, high-dose corticosteroids or biologics, primary immunodeficiency. Also: thymus disorder (thymoma, thymectomy, myasthenia gravis) and anaphylaxis to egg, chicken protein or gelatin. Precautions: age 6–8 months, age ≥60 years, pregnancy and breastfeeding, asymptomatic HIV with CD4 200–499.

c) (1) Advise deferring or avoiding travel to the yellow fever endemic/transmission area if at all possible, or substituting a non-endemic destination. (2) If travel is unavoidable, emphasize rigorous mosquito bite avoidance against the day-biting Aedes aegypti: DEET or icaridin repellent, permethrin-treated clothing, long sleeves and trousers, air-conditioned or screened accommodation, bed nets, and avoidance of peridomestic standing water. (3) Provide a signed Medical Contraindication to Vaccination waiver on the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, and warn that the destination or a transit country may refuse entry, quarantine the traveller, or vaccinate at the border regardless of the waiver. (4) Counsel on the symptoms of yellow fever and the need to seek medical care promptly, and review other required travel immunizations and malaria chemoprophylaxis.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Yellow Book / WHO IHR: waiver documented on the ICVP; single lifetime dose now considered valid for life for most travellers.

cohort_answer.text: A) YEL-AND (neurotropic disease - meningoencephalitis, ADEM, GBS, acute bulbar palsy; incidence 0.8/100,000, higher risk <6 months and older adults, onset 4-23 days post-vaccine, usually recovers, rare fatality). YEL-AVD (viscerotropic disease - severe illness/multi-organ failure resembling wild-type YF, onset 2-5 days post-vaccine, risk increases with age, case fatality 65% overall higher in women, linked to thymus disease/older age). B) Infants <6 months of age; immunocompromised; thymus disease (thymoma, thymectomy, myasthenia gravis); pregnancy/lactation; anaphylaxis; not recommended >60 years of age. C) Avoid travel if possible; mosquito repellent (DEET), permethrin-treated clothes, long sleeves, avoid standing water; will require International Certificate of Medical Contraindication to Vaccination if travel cannot be avoided; advise medical waiver may not be accepted by destination country.

questions.question: Zika virus.

parts.text: What percentage of patients are symptomatic?
List four ways it can be transmitted.
List three neurologic complications in adults.

parts_raw.text: A) What % of patients are symptomatic?
B) List 4 ways to transmit
C) List 3 neurological complications in adults

questions.model_answer: a) About 20% (roughly 1 in 5); the majority (~80%) of infections are asymptomatic. b) (1) Mosquito/vector-borne (Aedes aegypti, also A. albopictus), (2) sexual transmission, (3) blood transfusion, (4) perinatal/mother-to-child (including transplacental). c) (1) Guillain-Barre syndrome, (2) meningoencephalitis/encephalitis, (3) transverse myelitis.
questions.beyond_mandell: The ~20% symptomatic figure and the specific adult neuro complications beyond GBS are established teaching/CDC data; the chapter documents the transmission routes (p. 2024) and GBS (p. 2027) but does not state the exact symptomatic percentage.

cohort_answer.text: A) 20% symptomatic (80% asymptomatic). B) Vector-borne (mosquito); Sexual transmission (all kinds); Blood transfusion; Mother-to-child transmission; Organ transplant; Lab exposure. C) Guillain barre syndrome; Encephalitis; Meningoencephalitis; Transverse myelitis; Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy; Transient sensorineural hearing loss; Brain ischemia; Neuropsychiatric/cognitive symptoms.

questions.question: Dengue.

parts.text: What is the vector?
Discuss the environmental factors that would increase transmission.
Discuss the effect of a second infection with dengue.

parts_raw.text: A) What is the vector?
B) Discuss the environmental factors that would increase transmission?
C) Discuss the effect of a second infection with dengue

questions.model_answer: a) Aedes aegypti (principal vector); Aedes albopictus (and A. polynesiensis) can also transmit. b) Warm climate/rising temperature (enhances viral replication in the mosquito and is expanding the vector range with global warming); rainfall and humidity; and abundant peridomestic standing-water breeding sites (uncovered water storage, discarded containers, tires) in crowded urbanized settings with poor vector control. c) A secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype predisposes to severe dengue/DHF: cross-reactive non-neutralizing antibody plus memory T cells drive antibody-dependent enhancement and a cytokine/complement response causing vascular endothelial dysfunction and plasma leakage; relative risk of DHF with shock in secondary vs primary infection is as high as 100.

cohort_answer.text: A) Aedes aegypti (predominant), Aedes albopictus. B) Standing water (breeding sites); rainy season (higher precipitation/humidity). C) 4 serotypes exist; exposure to a previous serotype results in non-neutralizing antibody plus memory CD4/CD8 T cells causing more robust response to secondary infection; robust complement response causes cytokine release resulting in vascular endothelial dysfunction and plasma leakage (severe dengue). Dengue vaccine only in children 9-16 after confirmation of prior infection; can trigger severe dengue if not previously exposed.

questions.question: Complete a viral characteristics table.

parts.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika.

parts_raw.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika

questions.model_answer:
Mumps: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive).
Measles: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A adjunct; ribavirin unproven).
Hepatitis B: DNA; enveloped; yes - nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir), peginterferon.
EBV: DNA; enveloped; no established antiviral (aciclovir/ganciclovir have limited activity).
Ebola: RNA; enveloped; yes - monoclonal antibodies (atoltivimab-maftivimab-odesivimab [Inmazeb], ansuvimab [Ebanga]).
Zika: RNA; enveloped; none.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only measles (RNA, enveloped, ribavirin unproven, Mandell p. 2116) is covered by this chapter; the other rows are from general virology and current IDSA/CDC therapeutics.
